scenes.text: On the surface of Venus, it's about four hundred and sixty-five degrees Celsius.
Hot enough to melt lead. Day and night, at the poles and at the equator.
The air presses down ninety times harder than on Earth. Like being nearly a kilometre under the sea.
In 1982, a Soviet lander called Venera 13 touched down on that surface.
It was built to survive for half an hour. It lasted a little over two hours. Then it went silent.
And yet, some engineers at NASA argue that the most Earth-like conditions anywhere beyond our own planet are right here.
Not on the surface. Fifty kilometres above it.
Most plans to live on another planet are about Mars. So let's do something a little unusual. Let's keep score. Venus against Mars.
First, where exactly would we live? As you rise from the surface, the air gets thinner and cooler.
At fifty kilometres, the pressure is almost exactly what you feel at sea level on Earth. But the temperature is still about seventy-five degrees.
Go five kilometres higher, and it drops to about room temperature.
Now the pressure is about half of what we're used to. Roughly what climbers feel at Everest Base Camp.
So there's no single perfect altitude. There's a band, a few kilometres thick, where you choose your compromise.
Inside that band, you wouldn't need a pressure suit. You wouldn't freeze, and you wouldn't boil.
You'd still need a sealed mask with your own air supply, because the atmosphere is carbon dioxide. And protection from the clouds, for reasons we'll get to.
So, point one. Gravity. Venus is almost the same size as Earth, and its gravity is about ninety percent of ours.
On Mars, it's thirty-eight percent.
Nobody has ever lived in gravity like that. We don't know what years of it would do to bones, to muscles, or to a child growing up there.
On Venus, you'd weigh nearly as much as you do at home. Venus one, Mars nil.
Point two. Radiation. Venus has no magnetic field to protect it. Neither does Mars.
But at fifty kilometres on Venus, there is more air above your head than there is above a beach on Earth.
About a kilogram of air on every square centimetre. Enough to block much of the radiation coming in from space.
On Mars, there's less than two percent of that. That's why many plans for Mars bury their habitats under soil.
Venus two, Mars nil.
Point three, and this is the strange one. How does a city stay up in the sky?
On Earth, a balloon rises when it's filled with a gas that's lighter than the air around it. Helium, or hydrogen.
But the atmosphere of Venus is almost entirely carbon dioxide. And carbon dioxide is heavy.
About half as heavy again as the nitrogen and oxygen we breathe.
Which means that on Venus, the air we breathe is a lifting gas.
Fill a giant envelope with ordinary breathable air, and it floats.
At fifty kilometres, every cubic metre of it lifts about half a kilogram. About half of what helium lifts on Earth. Higher up, where it's cooler, it's closer to a quarter.
Not much on its own. But build it large enough, and it can carry the people living inside it.
In fact, they could live inside the lifting gas itself. The whole balloon would be one enormous room full of air.
And there's a bonus. The city would keep its air at the same pressure as outside.
Higher up, that's only about half of Earth's pressure. So the mix would get extra oxygen, and each breath would carry as much as it does at sea level.
With the same pressure inside and out, the envelope doesn't have to hold anything in.
Punch a hole in it, and there's no explosive decompression. The air just seeps out, slowly, and carbon dioxide seeps in.
One NASA engineer estimated that even a large rip would take thousands of hours to leak a significant amount of air.
On Mars, the air outside is less than one percent of the pressure on Earth. A hole means your air is escaping into almost nothing. Venus three, Mars nil.
And this isn't entirely theoretical. In 1985, two Soviet spacecraft, Vega 1 and Vega 2, flew past Venus on their way to Halley's Comet.
Each of them dropped a balloon into the clouds.
They floated about fifty-four kilometres up, for roughly two days, radioing data back to Earth.
In that time, the winds carried them at nearly two hundred and fifty kilometres an hour, a third of the way around the planet.
They were small, and they were filled with helium. But they proved something important.
We have already flown balloons on Venus. We just haven't sent people.
NASA engineers have thought about that next step. A study called HAVOC sketched a crewed airship a hundred and twenty-nine metres long.
Two astronauts would live on board for a month, fifty kilometres above the surface.
The airship would have to unfold and inflate while it was still falling through the atmosphere.
It was a study, never an approved mission. But it showed that the idea can be worked through with real engineering.
So, three nil to Venus. Which raises an awkward question.
If Venus wins this easily, why is almost every plan you've ever heard of about Mars?
Because so far, we've only counted what Venus is good at.
Point four. The clouds. They aren't made of water. They're made of droplets of concentrated sulphuric acid.
And our comfortable band sits right among them.
Metal corrodes. Seals fail. Anything that isn't protected slowly gets eaten.
The good news is that we know materials that survive acid. Chemists have kept sulphuric acid in glass for centuries.
In one NASA test, a thin film of Teflon spent a month in concentrated sulphuric acid. It still let through about ninety percent of the light, as much as on day one.
A sample of ordinary PVC started turning brown within an hour.
But a film in a lab is not a city in a storm, for decades. It would need constant repair.
Mars has its problems, but its atmosphere won't dissolve your house. Venus three, Mars one.
Point five. Power. Venus is closer to the Sun, so above the clouds, sunlight is almost twice as strong as on Earth.
And the clouds below reflect so much of it that a solar panel pointing down would work almost as well as one pointing up.
But there's a catch. The planet turns once every two hundred and forty-three days. The air does not.
At the height of our city, the atmosphere races around Venus in about six or seven days.
And a floating city moves with it. So night doesn't last twelve hours. It lasts around three days.
Three days with no sunlight, running on batteries. On Mars, a day lasts twenty-four hours and forty minutes.
Venus three, Mars two.
Point six. Water. Venus is one of the driest places we know. Its atmosphere holds about twenty parts per million of water vapour.
But there's a twist. Those droplets aren't pure acid. They contain water too.
In principle, we could recover it by processing the sulphuric acid.
It would take a lot of energy, and nobody has built a machine to do it there.
Mars has water too, frozen as ice in the ground. You can dig it up.
Oxygen is the easier part. In 2021, a small experiment called MOXIE pulled oxygen straight out of the carbon dioxide on Mars.
The same trick would work on Venus. But for water, Mars has the easier source. Venus three, Mars three.
Point seven. The ground. On Mars, you can stand on rock. You can dig, build, and mine whatever the planet has.
On Venus, everything you build with has to come from the air, or from Earth.
The surface is right there, fifty kilometres below. And nothing we've sent has survived on it for more than about two hours.
Our balloons lasted about two days. On Mars, rovers have been driving around for decades.
Venus three, Mars four.
Point eight. Getting there. And here, Venus wins again.
Launch windows open about every year and a half, instead of every two years or so for Mars.
And a round trip, with a month spent at Venus, could take as little as fourteen months. The same short visit to Mars takes a year and a half or more. Four all.
But the score hides the hardest part of all. Getting home.
To leave Mars, you launch from the ground, on a small planet, with weak gravity.
To leave Venus, you launch a rocket hanging from a balloon, on a planet almost as heavy as Earth.
To reach orbit there, you have to go about twice as fast as you would at Mars.
We've never even launched a rocket from Mars. It's one of the reasons bringing back a single rock is so hard. On Venus, it's harder still.
So that's the real answer. Mars isn't more Earth-like. In many ways, Venus is.
But Mars gives you ground to dig, ice to melt, and a way back home.
Mars offers a place to stand. Venus offers a place to float.
And maybe one day, someone will look out of a window over an endless sea of yellow clouds.
Breathing ordinary air, at room temperature, in almost ordinary gravity. With a furnace fifty kilometres beneath their feet.
So here's a question for you. Would you rather live in a cave on Mars, or in a balloon above Venus? Let me know in the comments.
